He has already given a real school name, so what he says next will be believed.
Sounding relaxed is what Marchetti said a cover story is for.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: He does know that the education office is on the third floor, that it does not open until half past ten, and that Ferris would have to leave her desk to find out.
Marchetti wrote it out that morning and said a cover story should be boring enough that nobody asks a second question.
So Jonah says the letter went to the education office last week, and that he is happy to wait in the lobby while she phones them.
She asks which school he is from, and he tells her without any trouble at all.

distractorRationale.1: That is Jonah speaking, not the story telling you something is true.  What a character says out loud is a move they are making, and one sentence later we learn he has no idea.
distractorRationale.2: An answer that went smoothly does not buy credit for the next one.  Ferris asks the harder question straight afterwards, which is how you know it did not.
distractorRationale.3: That is the general rule about being boring, and the question asks about this particular offer.  A rule explains why he stays calm; it does not explain why the offer works.

items.explain: The offer is safe because checking it is expensive for Ferris and free for Jonah.  A shut office, a third floor, and a desk she would have to leave are the whole of it.  What a character says is not evidence that it is true, and an earlier smooth answer buys nothing for a later one.

items.stem: Why does Jonah write the real time, ten fifteen, on the visitor log when the name he writes is false?
choices: The visitor log gets checked against the clock at the front desk.
A lie is easier to keep straight later when part of it is genuinely true.
He wants Ferris to see that he arrived before the museum got busy.
Marchetti's card told him to write down the time of the number fourteen bus.

distractorRationale.0: Nobody in the story checks the log against anything.  You gave the museum a system the text never mentions.
distractorRationale.2: The story never says the museum gets busy, or that Jonah cares when it does.  Watch for reasons that sound sensible and are not on the page.
distractorRationale.3: The card has the bus on it, not a time.  Read the eleven words the story actually gives you before deciding what they told him to do.

items.explain: A true detail inside a false story is one fewer thing to keep straight, which is why the real time sits underneath the fake name.  The other answers each add a system, a motive, or an instruction that the story never puts on the page.

items.stem: This story is told about Jonah rather than by him.  What does that let the reader see?
choices: What both Jonah and Ines are thinking, the whole way through the story
Only what somebody standing in the doorway of the room could see
What Marchetti makes of each sheet as he collects it
Jonah's mind, with Ines's reasons hidden until he reads them

distractorRationale.0: Ines's thinking never appears.  All we get of her is what she writes and what she says out loud, and Jonah has to read her sheet upside down to get even that much.
distractorRationale.1: Somebody in the doorway could not know that Jonah finds Ines mildly insulting, or that he has been planning to say it was easy since the stairs.  The story goes inside one head.
distractorRationale.2: Marchetti collects the sheets without reading a single one, and the story never opens his thoughts.  What he makes of it is exactly what Jonah, and the reader, cannot see.

items.explain: The story stays inside Jonah.  Ines is given no thoughts at all, which is why he has to read her sheet upside down to find out what she wrote, and Marchetti hands his back with no expression.  That limit is what makes the ending land.

items.stem: Jonah asks for his sheet back and adds one more line.  What has he worked out?
choices: He has decided the thirty seconds on the landing were dangerous after all.
He wants Marchetti to see that his sheet is now longer than the one Ines wrote.
A log that skips what he could not explain is no use to the next reader.
He is copying Ines, because hers was the sheet that got read.

distractorRationale.0: The line he writes says cause unknown and no action taken.  He still does not know what the sound was; what changed is that he wrote it down anyway.
distractorRationale.1: Marchetti collects the sheets without reading a single one, and says so.  Length cannot be the point of something nobody marks.
distractorRationale.3: Nobody's sheet got read.  Ines shows him what a complete log looks like, which is not the same as him copying her to be noticed.

items.explain: Jonah adds the line because Marchetti has just said who a log is for.  It is not for the marker, because nobody marks it.  It is for the next person standing on a landing, and the least impressive sentence on the sheet is the only one that helps them.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that report something happening inside the narrator's own head, rather than something anybody sitting in that van could have seen.
spans: I watch those doors the way you watch a kettle that is refusing to boil.
It only feels safe because if I call it and I am wrong, the exercise dies quietly, everybody goes home early, and nothing bad ever happens to me.
A man in a green jacket goes in and does not come out.
Two women come out with a folded stroller between them.
I sit in a parked van with a radio, a stopwatch, and a paper map, and I write down times.
items.explain: Two of these report something only the narrator could know: a comparison nobody else hears, and a motive nobody else could see.  The van, the man in the green jacket, and the women with the stroller would all have shown up on a camera.

items.stem: Tap the three phrases that belong to the part Jonah did not write down at first.  The others were on his sheet from the start.
spans: on the second floor landing
heard a door close
did absolutely nothing
contact with front desk staff
the folder located and photographed
exit at ten forty-one
items.explain: Everything on the first sheet is true, and the thirty seconds on the landing is what is missing from it.  A door, a rail, and half a minute of doing nothing are the whole omission, and Jonah only writes them down once Marchetti has explained who the log is for.

items.stem: Jonah's offer to wait works because of things he knows and Ferris does not.  Choose the three the story actually gives him.
choices: The permission letter really was sent to the office last week
Ferris would have to leave her desk to find out
What he offered can be checked, so it does not sound invented on the spot
Ferris has already telephoned his school once that morning
The education office does not open until half past ten
There is nobody else at the front desk who could cover for her

distractorRationale.0: Jonah has no idea whether that letter exists.  What a character says out loud is not automatically true, even when saying it works.
distractorRationale.3: Ferris never telephones anybody in this story.  Adding that makes the moment far safer than it was, and the risk that she might is the whole scene.
distractorRationale.5: The story never says whether anyone else works that desk.  It is a fair guess, and this question is asking for what is on the page instead.

items.explain: Three facts sit behind the offer and Jonah holds all three: the office is shut, it is two floors up, and checking it means abandoning the desk.  A guess about staffing and a hope about a letter are not the same kind of thing at all.

items.stem: Complete the sentence about how this story is told.  The reader is given Jonah's thoughts about the landing, but of Ines we get only {{0}}, which is why her reasoning has to be read {{1}} before Jonah understands what a complete log looks like.

choices: what Marchetti says about her
everything she is feeling
what he can see and hear
out loud to the whole room
upside down across the table
once the whole debrief has ended

items.explain: The story gives Jonah's thoughts and gives Ines only what he can see and hear, which is why her reasoning arrives sideways, read upside down across a table.  A narrator's limits are part of what a story is doing rather than an accident of the telling.

items.stem: Marchetti says a log is only ever for one person.  In four words or fewer, who is that?
items.explain: Marchetti says the logs are not marked and never have been, so a log is not written for him.  It is written for whoever is next on a landing, wondering whether a sound they just heard matters.

partA.stem: The ninety-minute result in Source A comes with one detail that should make a reader slow down before believing it.  Which detail?
choices: The beacon sends out a coded pulse instead of a plain one.
The company has only been making rescue gear for nineteen years.
The people who ran the test are the people who sell the beacon.
The beacon is light enough to clip onto a belt.

partB.stem: Which sentence from Source A best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Corvid Systems has been building rescue gear for nineteen years and stands behind this product completely.
Our own engineers ran that test in the Halloway service tunnel with the receiver at the surface entrance.
It clips to a belt or a pack strap and weighs eleven ounces.
It sends out a coded pulse on a very low frequency.

distractorRationale.0: A coded pulse is how the beacon works, not a reason to doubt the number.  You went looking for something technical when the problem is who did the measuring.
distractorRationale.1: Nineteen years is offered as a reason to trust the company, and you read it as a reason to doubt them.  Length of experience does not tell you who was holding the stopwatch.
distractorRationale.3: The weight is a fact about the object that anyone could check on a scale.  It has nothing to do with whether the ninety minutes is real.

items.explain: A test result is only as good as the tester is free to report a bad one.  Corvid designs, builds, and sells the Wren-7, and Corvid engineers ran this test, so the people checking the claim are the people making it.  That is the tell, and Source B is what an outside test of the same tunnel looks like.

partA.stem: Source A ran its test in one tunnel.  Which of its statements claims more than one tunnel could ever show?
choices: That low frequencies get through rock better than ordinary radio frequencies do.
That what worked at Halloway will now work everywhere.
That the beacon is about the size of a deck of cards.
That the signal stayed strong enough for the receiver to report a position.

partB.stem: Which sentence from Source A best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: The signal never once dropped below the level the receiver needs to report a position.
Low frequencies were chosen because they pass through solid rock far better than the frequencies ordinary radios use.
Any tunnel in the country can now be worked with confidence.
The Wren-7 is a beacon about the size of a deck of cards.

distractorRationale.0: That is a general fact about radio and the reason the beacon was designed this way.  It was true before this test and does not rest on it.
distractorRationale.2: A size is measured with a ruler, not in a tunnel.  It would read the same whether the test went well or badly.
distractorRationale.3: That sentence reports what happened during the test itself, which is exactly what a test is allowed to say.  A strong result is not the same thing as an overclaim.

items.explain: One test in one tunnel can tell you what happened in that tunnel.  The brief reports its run honestly and then takes a step it has not earned, from forty feet of Halloway stone to every tunnel in the country.  Source B tests the very same tunnel and gets nine minutes, which is how a reader finds out that the step was too big.

partA.stem: Source B reports that the signal lasted nine minutes.  Which detail tells a reader that the nine minutes itself was recorded carefully?
choices: Two instructors, Marchetti and Osei, signed their names to the entry at the bottom.
The receiver's battery was replaced with a fresh one before every run.
The staff will look at the entry again once the summer exercises are finished.
Two people timed the same run on their own and came out within three seconds of each other.

partB.stem: Which sentence from Source B best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Its battery was replaced before each run.
This entry will be reviewed again after the summer exercises.
It is dated the fourteenth of March and signed by two instructors, Marchetti and Osei.
Two observers wrote the times down separately, and their times differ by no more than three seconds.

distractorRationale.0: A signature tells you who wrote the entry, not how the time was taken.  Two names at the bottom are not two stopwatches.
distractorRationale.1: A fresh battery rules out one cause of a short signal, which is careful work on the equipment.  The question is about the number, and a battery cannot check a number.
distractorRationale.2: A promise to look again later says nothing about how the measurement was taken today.  Reviewing a figure in the summer cannot make it more carefully timed in March.

items.explain: Careful measuring means somebody could have caught you getting it wrong.  Two observers writing the time down separately and landing within three seconds is that check, because one stopwatch held by one person cannot be checked by anybody.  Everything else in this list is good practice around the number rather than a check on it.

partA.stem: Source B measured nine minutes where Source A promised ninety.  Why does Source B still refuse to call the Wren-7 a bad beacon?
choices: They are keeping the hardwired line, so the beacon does not matter to them.
The bend and the damp walls prove the beacon was never the problem.
Two runs in one tunnel cannot settle how the beacon behaves anywhere else.
The staff think nine minutes is long enough for the work they do.

partB.stem: Which sentence from Source B best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: The staff recommend that the site keep its hardwired line and treat the beacon as a second method rather than a replacement.
A tool that works for nine minutes is genuinely useful.
Two runs in one tunnel is nowhere near enough evidence for a statement that broad.
The staff note two local conditions that may explain the gap between these results and the maker's claim.

distractorRationale.0: Keeping the line is what they recommend, not the reason behind it.  They also say to treat the beacon as a second method, which is a long way from saying it does not matter.
distractorRationale.1: The staff say the bend and the damp may explain the gap.  Turning a possible explanation into a proof is the same move Source A makes, and Source B is careful not to make it.
distractorRationale.3: The log does say nine minutes is useful, which is about what the tool is worth rather than about how far the evidence reaches.  You answered why they still like it instead of why they will not judge it.

items.explain: Source B holds itself to the rule Source A breaks.  It has two runs in one tunnel, so it reports what those two runs showed and refuses to turn them into a verdict on the beacon anywhere else.  Measuring a small number does not entitle you to a big claim any more than measuring a large one does.

items.stem: The small print at the bottom of Source A says test results depend on local conditions.  What does that line do to the brief's biggest claim?
choices: It proves the brief is honest, so a team can trust the ninety minutes it promises.
It means the beacon will not work anywhere except Halloway.
It quietly takes back the part of the claim the large print made loudest.
It applies only to the parts about water, dust, and impact.

distractorRationale.0: Printing a limit is better than hiding one, and it still does not make the number bigger.  Honest about a weakness and right about a result are two different things.
distractorRationale.1: It depends on conditions is not the same as it fails everywhere else.  You turned a limit on a claim into the opposite claim.
distractorRationale.3: The line says test results, and the ninety minutes is the test result.  Reading it as though it covered only the rugged bits is choosing whichever reading costs the brief the least.

items.explain: The headline says any tunnel in the country and the small print says results depend on local conditions, and both are on the same page in the same document.  The two cannot both be true, so the brief is arguing against itself before anyone else gets a turn.  Source B is simply the tunnel where that argument gets settled.

items.stem: A team is deciding what to carry into the Halloway tunnel next week.  The maker's brief promises ninety minutes and this log measured nine.  Which source should the team plan around?
choices: The brief, because ninety minutes is the safer number for a team to plan around.
The log, because two people timed its runs and it has nothing to sell.
Neither, because two sources that disagree cancel each other out.
The brief, because it was written by the engineers who built the beacon.

distractorRationale.0: Planning around the bigger number is the opposite of safe.  A team that expects ninety minutes and gets nine is stranded at exactly the moment the plan says everything is fine.
distractorRationale.2: Two sources that disagree are a reason to look at how each one was made, not a reason to give up.  One of these named its rock type, its date, and two separate timekeepers, and the other named none of them.
distractorRationale.3: The engineers who built it also sell it, and theirs is the test nobody outside the company watched.  Knowing how a thing was made does not make you the right person to judge it.

items.explain: Both sources tested the same tunnel, which is what makes this decidable rather than a matter of opinion.  The log names its depth, its rock type, its date, and two independent timekeepers; the brief names only a depth, and it sells the beacon.  For a team walking into Halloway, both numbers claim to be about their tunnel, and only the log was timed by two people with nothing to sell.

items.stem: Which of these can a reader NOT check about the test in Source A?
choices: How deep the beacon was.
Which tunnel it was run in.
Where the receiver was placed.
When the test was run.

distractorRationale.0: Forty feet of stone is right there in the sentence about the test.  A reader who decides nothing is checkable stops looking before finding the things that are.
distractorRationale.1: The brief names the Halloway service tunnel, and naming it is what let the training staff test the very same one.
distractorRationale.2: The brief says the receiver sat at the surface entrance.  That detail is what makes the log's note about the bend at twenty-five feet worth reading.

items.explain: Source A gives the depth, the tunnel, and the position of the receiver, and it never gives a date.  That one hole matters more than it looks, because a result with no date cannot be lined up against anything measured before or after it.  The brief carries a document number, so leaving the date off was a choice rather than an oversight.

items.stem: Tap the three sentences where Source A stops describing the beacon and starts asking for the sale.
spans: We are confident that once your team has carried a Wren-7 they will not want to go back into a tunnel without one.
In testing, the Wren-7 held a clear signal through forty feet of stone for the full ninety minutes of its battery life.
Contact our sales office for volume pricing and to arrange a live test at your own site.
It switches on with one control that a gloved hand can find without looking.
No other beacon anywhere near this price comes close to that result.
Setup takes under a minute, and the receiver reads out a distance as well as a direction.
items.explain: A document can describe a real product and still be an advertisement, so the useful split is not honest against dishonest.  Three of these describe the beacon and three ask you to buy it: one promises how your team will feel, one gives you the sales office, and one measures the beacon against every rival on the market.  A reader who notices the switch reads the numbers more slowly.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that describe the Halloway tunnel itself rather than the beacon or the test.
spans: The surface receiver held the signal for nine minutes and then lost it.
That time the receiver lost the signal after seven minutes.
The Halloway tunnel bends sharply at the twenty-five foot level.
The receiver was the unit supplied with the beacons.
Both runs were timed with a stopwatch.
The tunnel is also cut through wet limestone rather than dry granite, and the walls are damp along most of their length.
items.explain: The staff keep two kinds of fact apart: what the beacon did, and what the ground around it was like.  A bend at twenty-five feet and wet limestone walls belong to the tunnel and would still be there with a different beacon in hand.  Naming them is what lets a reader ask whether nine minutes is a fact about the Wren-7 or a fact about Halloway.

items.stem: Choose the three things about Source A that a careful reader would list as reasons to check its ninety-minute claim somewhere else.
choices: The test was run by the same company that sells the beacon
The test lasted only ninety minutes, which is a short time to run a test
The brief gives a document number and no date at all
The beacon takes the standard battery cell a department already stocks
One tunnel was tested and every tunnel in the country was concluded about
The brief names the tunnel the test was run in

distractorRationale.1: Ninety minutes is the whole life of the battery, so the test ran for as long as the beacon can run.  You read a limit of the device as a shortcut taken by the tester.
distractorRationale.3: A common battery is convenient and tells you nothing about whether the signal held.  This is a fact about the product where the question asks about the evidence.
distractorRationale.5: Naming the tunnel is the most checkable thing the brief does, and it is the reason the training staff could test the very same one.  You flagged the part that helps you.

items.explain: Three problems sit in Source A and all three are about the evidence rather than the equipment: who ran the test, when it was run, and how far the conclusion travels past it.  The specifications are not the issue at all, and naming the tunnel is the one move the brief makes that a checker can actually use.

items.stem: Complete a reader's note on the two sources.  The maker's brief and this log tested {{0}}, which is what makes their disagreement something to settle rather than a matter of opinion, and the log is the better guide for a team going into Halloway because it {{1}}.

choices: in the same month
the same tunnel
the same number of beacons
reaches the more cautious of the two conclusions
was written by people who work underground
names the conditions behind its numbers

items.explain: The two sources are comparable because they tested the same tunnel, so one of them has to be wrong about it.  The log wins on method rather than on tone: it gives its depth, its rock, its date, and two timekeepers.  A cautious conclusion with no conditions behind it would be worth no more than a confident one.

items.stem: Match each hole in Source A to what that particular hole costs a reader.
rowLabels: A document number with no date anywhere on the page
A test run by the maker's own engineers
One tunnel tested, every tunnel concluded about
colLabels: The people who checked the claim are the people selling it
The result cannot be lined up against anything else that was measured
The conclusion travels further than the evidence underneath it
items.explain: Three different holes with three different consequences, and they are not interchangeable.  A missing date stops you comparing, a maker running its own test removes the outside check, and a claim about every tunnel outruns a test in one.  Naming which hole you have found is how you decide what the source can still be used for.

partA.stem: Reading the three tunnel results together changes what any one of them means.  What do the three together show?
choices: Dry granite is the only rock a beacon can be used in.
The beacon is unreliable, because two of the three tunnels went badly for it.
The ground the beacon sits in explains the differences, not the beacon.
Depth is what decides how long a signal lasts.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the article best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: A beacon at the thirty foot level lost contact there after eight minutes.
The first tunnel was cut through dry granite and ran almost straight for two hundred feet.
Depth is the third, and it is the one everybody thinks of first.
Read together, they say something different, which is that the beacon is not the thing that changed.

distractorRationale.0: Granite is where the best result happened, so it is easy to read it as the only rock that works.  The third tunnel was limestone and held for fifty-one minutes, which breaks that rule.
distractorRationale.1: Two poor results out of three feels like a verdict, and it is the reading the article warns against in its very next sentence.  Counting outcomes is not the same as comparing conditions.
distractorRationale.3: Depth is on the list, and the article says outright that it is not the whole story.  Water and the shape of the path matter too.

items.explain: The same beacon behaved three different ways, so whatever changed was not the beacon.  Depth, the shape of the path and water are all properties of the ground, so the ground is what explains the differences.

partA.stem: The tag report in this level says heat and cold both cost a battery runtime, but in different ways.  What does this tunnel article say about how a sharp bend and greater depth cost a beacon its range?
choices: A bend costs range mainly when the rock around it is also wet
Depth costs more, since it is the one that everybody thinks of first
They do the same work, because both put more rock in the signal's way
A bend helps the signal by letting it follow the open passage

partB.stem: Which sentence from the article best supports your answer?
choices: That extra rock does the same work that greater depth would do.
A sharp bend forces the signal to cut the corner through solid material instead of following the open passage.
A damp limestone wall can cost a team more range than another ten feet of depth would.
Depth is the third, and it is the one everybody thinks of first.

distractorRationale.0: The article treats water and the bend as two separate conditions.  A bend costs range because the signal cuts through solid rock, wet or dry.
distractorRationale.1: Thinking of depth first is the habit the article corrects.  It says the extra rock a bend adds does the same work that depth does, not less.
distractorRationale.3: It is the other way round:  the article says a bend makes the signal leave the open passage and go through rock.

items.explain: The tag report sets two costs side by side and says they work differently.  This article sets two costs side by side and says they work the same way:  a sharp bend makes the signal cut through extra rock, and that extra rock does the same work that greater depth would do.

partA.stem: A team has to write one sentence of advice for buyers and back it with this article.  Which sentence can the article actually support?
choices: Do not buy these beacons, because in one tunnel the signal was lost after only eight minutes.
Buy the beacon that performed best in dry granite.
Run your test in your easiest, driest tunnel so the beacon gets a fair chance to do its best.
Ask what the depth, the rock, and the shape of the passage were before believing a beacon's number.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the article would you quote to back the answer you just gave?
choices: It is that a claim about beacon performance is close to meaningless unless it names the depth, the rock, and the shape of the passage.
The association recommends that every department run one test in its own worst tunnel rather than trusting a figure measured somewhere else.
The receiver at the entrance never lost it once.
Read on its own, each of those results looks like a verdict on the equipment.

distractorRationale.0: One tunnel losing the signal after eight minutes is a single outcome, and the article says outright that the beacon is not the thing that changed.  The line you would be quoting is the one describing the misreading.
distractorRationale.1: That result is real and it belongs to the granite rather than to the beacon.  Turning the best condition into a shopping rule is the mistake the article spends three paragraphs undoing.
distractorRationale.2: The line you would be leaning on recommends the opposite: test in your own worst tunnel.  Reversing a recommendation and citing it anyway is the fastest way to be caught.

items.explain: Using evidence means the sentence you wrote has to be the sentence your source will hold up.  The article's own conclusion names depth, rock, and shape, so a buyer's rule built on those three is supported line for line.  A rule built on the best result quietly drops the conditions that produced it.

partA.stem: Which conclusion goes further than this article's own evidence allows?
choices: Freezing air can drain a tag's battery far faster than mild air
Heat costs a battery runtime too, though in a different way
One runtime number describes one climate, not every climate
Every runtime number a maker shares should be doubted

partB.stem: Which sentence from the article best supports your answer?
choices: A battery loses much of its charge in freezing air, no matter which device it powers.
It wears the battery down a different way, over repeated hot stretches, rather than draining it all at once.
None of this means a buyer should doubt every runtime number a maker shares.
Two numbers measured in two different climates are not really being compared at all.

distractorRationale.0: The article says freezing air does exactly this to a battery, so this conclusion stays inside its evidence.
distractorRationale.1: The article says heat still costs runtime and wears the battery down a different way, over repeated hot stretches.
distractorRationale.2: That is the article's own lesson about comparing results, so it stays inside what the tests showed.

items.explain: A careful reader keeps what a source says apart from what it does not.  This article warns against trusting a single warm-weather number, but it stops well short of doubting every number a maker shares, and it says so in a sentence of its own:  none of this means a buyer should doubt every runtime number a maker shares.

items.stem: The tag report in this level tells a buyer who needs the tag to work in the cold to ask for the cold number, not the warmest one on offer.  How does this tunnel article's closing advice go further than that?
choices: It tells a department to trust the deepest result the association measured
It tells a buyer to pick the beacon that held up in the dry granite tunnel
It tells a department to run its own test, not trust a number from elsewhere
It tells a buyer to trust whichever number the beacon's maker publishes

distractorRationale.0: The article warns against exactly that.  Depth is the condition it says everybody thinks of first, and the association's own numbers show it is not the whole story.
distractorRationale.1: Choosing on one good run is reading a single number alone.  The article's point is that the granite result says more about the tunnel than about the beacon.
distractorRationale.3: The article says a number offered without its conditions cannot be checked, so it gives no reason to trust a maker's number as it stands.

items.explain: Both reports want a reader to get a number measured in the conditions they will really face.  The tag report says to ask for that number.  This article goes a step further and tells each department to run one test in its own worst tunnel, so the number is its own instead of one measured somewhere else.

items.stem: A buyer says the tag must be badly made, because it went silent in the mountains in just under three days.  Which line from the article answers that buyer most directly?
choices: A tag there lasted just under three days before it went silent, a runtime the board called far below every other test.
A battery loses much of its charge in freezing air, no matter which device it powers.
That is close to the maker's own thirty-day number, and a range a buyer could plan around.
The third test ran in a freezing mountain climate.

distractorRationale.0: That line is the result the buyer is pointing at.  Repeating it agrees with the buyer instead of answering them.
distractorRationale.2: The coastal number shows the tag can do well, but it does not say why the tag did badly in the mountains.
distractorRationale.3: Naming the climate tells you where the test ran.  It does not say that the cold, not the tag, cut the runtime.

items.explain: The buyer reads a cold-weather runtime as a verdict on the tag.  The line that answers them is the one about the battery:  freezing air drains a battery's charge no matter which device it powers, so the short runtime is a fact about the cold that would happen to any tag.

items.stem: The association published all three tunnel results side by side instead of reporting the best one.  Why does that make the results more useful?
choices: It shows the association is not being paid by the beacon's maker to hide bad results.
The differences show that the ground, not the beacon, is doing the work.
Three numbers averaged together give a more accurate figure than one number does.
It gives a buyer three chances to find a result they like and then quote that one.

distractorRationale.0: Publishing everything does suggest nobody is being protected, which is a fact about the association rather than about the results.  The question asks what the three together tell you.
distractorRationale.2: Averaging fifty-one minutes, eight minutes, and a full battery would hide the very thing the article found.  The spread is the finding, and an average is a way of throwing it away.
distractorRationale.3: That is what a buyer should not do with them, and the article says to ask for conditions before results.  Three numbers to choose between is the problem, not the point.

items.explain: One result reads as a verdict on the equipment and three read as an experiment.  The beacon is the constant across all three tunnels, so anything that changed has to be the ground, which is what lets the article name three conditions of the ground as the things that did.  Side by side is not a courtesy; it is the method.

items.stem: Tap the three sentences that explain how the ground itself acts on a signal.  The others are the article talking about its own report or about what you should do.
spans: It published all three results side by side, which turns out to be far more useful than any one of them alone.
Wet rock absorbs radio energy far more effectively than dry rock does.
The beacon there held for fifty-one minutes before the signal became unreliable.
A sharp bend forces the signal to cut the corner through solid material instead of following the open passage.
A team deciding what to buy should ask for the conditions of a test before asking for the result.
A damp limestone wall can cost a team more range than another ten feet of depth would.
items.explain: The article's central move is to separate the device from the ground it is used in, and these three sentences are where the ground does the explaining: wet rock turns signal into heat, a bend forces the signal through extra stone, and damp walls can cost more range than ten more feet of depth.  The other three are the article describing its own report and telling you what to do with it.

items.stem: A report can quote a measurement as a fact, but it must quote a judgment as someone's opinion.  Tap the three phrases that the association measured.
spans: far more useful than any one of them alone
held its signal for the full life of the battery
close to meaningless
lost contact there after eight minutes
a number that cannot be checked
held for fifty-one minutes before the signal became unreliable
items.explain: Three of these came off the tests:  a signal held for the battery's full life, contact lost after eight minutes, and a signal held for fifty-one minutes.  Far more useful, close to meaningless, and a number that cannot be checked are judgments the article makes about those results, and a careful report quotes them as judgments.

items.stem: Choose the three conclusions that go further than this article's results allow.
choices: The beacon is a poor product that buyers should avoid
Wet rock absorbs radio energy far more than dry rock
Depth has no effect on how far a signal travels
A sharp bend can cost a beacon some of its range
A result means little until its conditions are named
A beacon in dry rock keeps its signal the whole time

distractorRationale.1: The article says exactly this, and its wet tunnel is where the beacon did worst.
distractorRationale.3: Supported:  the article names the shape of the path as one of its three conditions and explains how a bend costs a beacon range.
distractorRationale.4: That is the article's own conclusion, drawn from its three results, so it does not reach past them.

items.explain: Each of the three goes past what the tests showed.  The article says its point is not that the beacons are good or bad.  It says depth clearly matters, even though it is not the whole story.  Its dry limestone tunnel still lost a reliable signal after fifty-one minutes, so dry rock is no guarantee.

items.stem: Finish the comparison.  The tag report in this level picks out cold as the clearest of its three factors.  This article puts {{0}} first among its own three, and it saves {{1}} for last, even though that is the one everybody thinks of first.

choices: the shape of the path
water
depth
water
the bend at twenty-five feet
depth

items.explain: Both reports list three conditions and trace their results to where each test ran.  This article names water first and the shape of the path second, and it puts depth third on purpose:  depth is the one everybody thinks of first, and the article's own numbers show it is not the whole story.

items.stem: Put the steps of the article's case in the order it makes them.
tiles: Name the three conditions that differed, every one a property of the ground
Report what the same beacon did in three different tunnels
Tell a buyer to ask for the conditions of a test before asking for its result
Point out that read together the results say the beacon is not what changed
items.explain: The article does not open with its advice, and that ordering is the argument.  Three results come first, then the observation that reading them together changes what they mean, then the three ground conditions that explain the spread, and only then the rule for a buyer.  Move the advice to the front and it is nothing but an opinion.

partA.stem: What is the central idea of "The Last Run"?
choices: That being a few minutes late can ruin a whole exercise
That strangers sitting near a café table are usually part of the exercise
That sticking to the plan means not gambling with the person
That the quickest way out of a station is the safest one

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports your answer?
choices: A man in a grey coat has taken the table beside Okafor's.
Afterward Marchetti asks why she was late, and Ines tells him about the man in the grey coat, the untouched cup, and the phone lying face down.
They walk the second route the way it was written, through the parking garage and up a ramp that seems a mile long, to the street where the car is waiting with its engine already running.
A plan is a promise to the person you are bringing out, and the promise is that you will not gamble with him.

distractorRationale.0: Marchetti says the opposite:  four minutes cost nothing, and she did the only right thing by being late.
distractorRationale.1: Marchetti says the man in the grey coat was a stranger with nothing to do with anyone.  The story's point is not about strangers.
distractorRationale.3: The story never praises speed.  They walk the second route the way it was written, and nobody runs.

items.explain: The story ends by naming its idea outright:  a plan is a promise to the person you are bringing out, and the promise is that you will not gamble with him.  Ines's four-minute delay keeps that promise.

items.stem: Why does Ines walk past the café door at nine forty instead of going in?
choices: She was early, and the plan had her wait until nine forty-two
She had left the folded newspaper on the train
Okafor waved her away from his table through the café's front window
A stranger by Okafor looked wrong, and she would not risk it

distractorRationale.0: She was on time:  the plan has her walking in at nine forty.  What she sees inside the café is what holds her back.
distractorRationale.1: The newspaper is still under her arm, and she later sets it on the counter.
distractorRationale.2: Okafor does nothing at all.  He stays at his table and gives no signal of any kind.

items.explain: Ines sees a man in a grey coat at the table beside Okafor's, reading nothing, his phone face down beside an untouched cup.  She cannot tell whether he matters, so she does not walk in, and she comes back the long way once he is gone.

partA.stem: At the café door, the newspaper under Ines's arm "feels as heavy as a brick."  What does that comparison suggest?
choices: Ines is getting cold from waiting outside in the wind
Ines is tired out from walking all the way across the station
Ines is planning to leave the newspaper behind somewhere
Ines feels the weight of the signal she is about to give

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports your answer?
choices: She walks past the door as if the café were any other shop, and she keeps walking until a shop window gives her the platform behind her.
He is sitting in the station café with a cold cup of tea.
The plan says Ines walks in at nine forty, with a folded newspaper carried under her arm, and Okafor follows her out at nine forty-two.
At nine forty-six she comes back the long way, past the ticket machines.

distractorRationale.0: Nothing in the story says she is cold.  The weight is in what the newspaper means, not in the weather.
distractorRationale.1: Nothing in the story says she is tired.  She comes back the long way past the ticket machines because she chooses to, not because she is worn out.
distractorRationale.2: The comparison is about how the newspaper feels at the door, not about where it ends up.  She keeps it under her arm as she walks past the door.

items.explain: The folded newspaper is the plan's signal:  the plan has Ines walk in with it at nine forty, and Okafor follows.  Calling it heavy as a brick shows how much that signal weighs on her at the door, because giving it would send Okafor out with her.

items.stem: Tap the three sentences that use figurative language instead of saying plainly what happens.
spans: He is sitting in the station café with a cold cup of tea.
She walks past the door as if the café were any other shop, and she keeps walking until a shop window gives her the platform behind her.
Ines's heart is running for both of them.
The plan says Ines walks in at nine forty, with a folded newspaper carried under her arm, and Okafor follows her out at nine forty-two.
Afterward Marchetti asks why she was late, and Ines tells him about the man in the grey coat, the untouched cup, and the phone lying face down.
They walk the second route the way it was written, through the parking garage and up a ramp that seems a mile long, to the street where the car is waiting with its engine already running.
items.explain: Three sentences say more than they literally mean:  a shop window gives her the platform behind her, her heart is running for both of them, and a ramp seems a mile long.  The other three report plainly what is there, what was planned, and what Ines tells Marchetti afterward.

partA.stem: While Ines stands at the café door, what does Jonah's scarf tell her?
choices: That Jonah has also spotted the man in the grey coat inside
That Jonah has seen nothing to stop the run
That Jonah wants her to call the whole run off now
That Jonah is getting cold out on the far platform

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports your answer?
choices: Jonah's scarf is still around his neck.
He is sitting in the station café with a cold cup of tea.
A man in a grey coat has taken the table beside Okafor's.
Ines does not go in.

distractorRationale.0: If Jonah had seen something wrong, he would have taken his scarf off.  It stays on.
distractorRationale.2: Taking the scarf off is the signal to stop, and Jonah has not done that.
distractorRationale.3: Nothing in the story says Jonah is cold.  The scarf matters as a signal:  taking it off would stop the run, and it is still on.

items.explain: Jonah's only job is to take off his scarf if anything looks wrong, which would stop the whole run.  His scarf is still around his neck, so from the platform he has seen nothing that calls for a stop.

items.stem: Okafor is not allowed to decide anything during the run.  How does that rule shape what Ines does at the café door?
choices: It means she must go in at nine forty, exactly as the plan says
It means she has to ask Marchetti before she changes the timing
It means Jonah must decide for her from the far platform
It means the choice to wait is hers alone, so she holds back

distractorRationale.0: She does not go in at nine forty, and Marchetti says holding back was the only right thing.  The rule only asks her not to hand the choice to Okafor.
distractorRationale.1: Nobody asks Marchetti anything during the run.  He asks her why she was late only afterward.
distractorRationale.2: Jonah has one job on the far platform, the scarf.  Nothing in the story has him deciding anything for Ines.

items.explain: The rule says the person being brought out never decides anything, so nothing at the door can be left to Okafor.  The choice falls on Ines alone, and she makes it herself by walking past the door and coming back later.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences where the story turns away from the plan.
spans: The person is Okafor, a quiet instructor who will spend the morning pretending to be frightened.
What actually happens is different.
Jonah's scarf is still around his neck.
Afterward Marchetti asks why she was late, and Ines tells him about the man in the grey coat, the untouched cup, and the phone lying face down.
Ines does not go in.
Nobody runs.
items.explain: The story sets out the plan first, then turns on two short sentences:  what actually happens is different, and Ines does not go in.  Everything after them follows from her choice at the door.

items.stem: Finish the description of how the story is built.  It opens with {{0}}, and it closes with {{1}}.

choices: the rule that Marchetti reads out twice
the car waiting at the top of the ramp
the man in the grey coat at the next table
Ines buying a bottle of water she does not want
Jonah taking off his scarf on the platform
Marchetti explaining why the delay was right

items.explain: The story is framed by Marchetti.  It opens with the rule he reads out twice, that the person being brought out never decides anything, and it closes with his verdict on the morning:  four minutes cost nothing.

partA.stem: Why does the note begin by comparing a person with a package?
choices: To show that packages are much harder to hide than people on a crowded street
To show that a person needs a faster route than a package does
To show that a package needs no plan card, unlike a person
To show that a person can get frightened, and a package cannot

partB.stem: Which sentence from the note best supports your answer?
choices: Every exfiltration starts with a plan card, and every line on it is settled before the day.
Moving a person is harder than moving a package.
It names a time limit, and if the pickup slips by more than ten minutes, the whole run is called off.
A package does not get frightened, change its mind, or decide halfway down a street that it would rather run.

distractorRationale.0: The note never says packages are hard to hide.  It says a person is harder to move, because a person can be frightened.
distractorRationale.1: Speed is not the point, and the note says nobody runs.  The difference is that a person can change their mind and a package cannot.
distractorRationale.2: The note says every exfiltration starts with a plan card.  It compares the two to explain why the person never decides, not to say who needs a card.

items.explain: The comparison sets up the note's first rule.  A package cannot get frightened, change its mind or decide to run, and a person can, so the whole exfiltration is planned around keeping every decision out of the moved person's hands.

items.stem: In five words or fewer, what does the stop signal outrank?
items.explain: The note puts the stop signal above every other line on the card, so it wins over the go signal, the routes and the time limit alike.  To outrank something is to rank higher than it.

items.stem: According to the note, why is the second route planned as carefully as the first?
choices: Because the second route usually turns out to be the faster one
Because the person being moved picks which route to take
Because a route that was only sketched is not really a route
Because the time limit starts counting on the second route

distractorRationale.0: Speed is not why.  Nobody runs on either route, and the note never says which is faster.
distractorRationale.1: The person being moved never decides anything, including the route.
distractorRationale.3: The ten-minute rule is about lateness, not about either route.  A second route that was only sketched is not really a route at all.

items.explain: A team that switches to its second route needs a real route, not a rough idea.  The note says a second route that was only sketched is not really a route at all, so it is planned as carefully as the first.

items.stem: Choose the three things the note says a plan card names before the day.
choices: a signal that means stop
the name of the person being moved
the officer who will lead the run
a time limit for the pickup
a fallback for another day
a password the person must say

distractorRationale.1: The card names signals, routes, a time limit and a fallback.  It never names the person.
distractorRationale.2: No officer's name is in the note's list of what the card names.
distractorRationale.5: The note lists no password among the card's lines:  only signals, routes, a time limit and a fallback.

items.explain: The card settles everything before the day:  the signal that means go, the signal that means stop, a first and a second route, a time limit, and a fallback for another day.

partA.stem: What problem does a dead drop solve?
choices: It lets the person hiding the item skip choosing a container, since any hiding spot will do.
It lets two people exchange something without being seen together at one place and time.
It lets the person loading the drop skip watching for followers, since the last rule is the collector's.
It lets a signal be sent instead of holding a face-to-face conversation.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: The signal says one thing only, that the drop is ready, and it says so from a distance, to someone walking past on the way to somewhere else.
The last rule belongs to the collector, not to whoever loaded the drop.
Nobody has to be caught in the same place at the same time as anybody else, and a connection nobody observed can never later be proven.
The container is the first decision.

distractorRationale.0: The container is the first decision, and the article spends a whole paragraph on it, so not just any hiding spot will do.  You are recalling a real detail attached to the wrong question.
distractorRationale.2: The last rule is aimed at the collector, and a rule about one person is not a free pass for the other.  The problem a dead drop solves is two people being seen together.
distractorRationale.3: A signal is one small piece of the method, the part that says a drop is ready. Removing the moment two people would be seen together is the actual point; the signal is just how the two sides arrange that.

items.explain: A dead drop solves the problem a meeting creates, which is that two people standing together can be tied together. Taking the second person out of that moment, not the container or the signal, is what the whole method is built around.

partA.stem: Why is a dead drop container built to look ordinary, like a bolt or a loose brick?
choices: To let the collector walk past it every day to check on it without drawing any attention.
To give anyone who notices it, by chance or on purpose, nothing worth a second look.
To hold a message written in a code that no stranger could read.
To spare the collector from standing in a public place, where someone might see the pickup.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: A good site is public enough that standing there for thirty seconds needs no excuse.
Each one means nothing to anyone who was not told to look.
A drop that draws a second glance has already failed, whether or not anyone opens it.
The collector cannot walk past the site every day just to check, because repetition is its own kind of pattern.

distractorRationale.0: Walking past the same spot every day is exactly the pattern the passage says a collector must avoid. An ordinary-looking container does not make daily visits safe.
distractorRationale.2: This passage never mentions codes or ciphers. Looking ordinary is about fooling a passerby's eyes, not about hiding writing from a reader.
distractorRationale.3: The passage says a good site is public enough to need no excuse for standing there. A hidden, non-public site is the opposite of what it recommends.

items.explain: A container is disguised so anyone who happens to notice it has no reason to look twice. That disguise has nothing to do with how often the site gets checked, what the container holds, or whether the site itself stays public.

partA.stem: Why do the two sides use a signal placed somewhere else, instead of just checking the drop site itself?
choices: Because a chalk mark or a strip of tape is faster to read than opening the container.
Because repeated visits to the site are a pattern a watcher could notice.
Because a signal lets the collector skip the slow, careful route that a pickup would need.
Because the last rule forbids the collector from going anywhere near the drop site.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: So the collector treats the pickup like a meeting that must be checked first: a slow route, a stop that shows what is behind, and a walk away with nothing retrieved if anything looks wrong.
The collector cannot walk past the site every day just to check, because repetition is its own kind of pattern.
The last rule belongs to the collector, not to whoever loaded the drop.
Instead the two sides agree on a signal placed somewhere else: a chalk mark on a lamppost, a strip of tape on a stop sign, or a plant moved from one side of a window to the other.

distractorRationale.0: That sentence lists what a signal can look like, not a claim about reading speed; the passage never compares how fast a signal is to read against opening a container.
distractorRationale.2: The slow route is still part of the pickup, because the passage says the collector treats it like a meeting that must be checked first.  The signal replaces the daily checking, not the careful walk.
distractorRationale.3: The last rule belongs to the collector, and it tells them how to visit the site, carefully, not to stay away.  A rule about the pickup cannot forbid the pickup.

items.explain: A signal exists because checking the drop site itself, over and over, would create a pattern a watcher could notice. Moving that repeated checking to a separate, everyday-looking spot is the entire reason the two-part system exists.

partA.stem: Why does the passage insist that the collector, not just the person who loaded the drop, must still take a slow, checked route to the pickup?
choices: Because going straight from the signal to the drop lets a follower watch one person do both things back to back.
Because the collector is more likely to be followed than the person who loaded the drop hours earlier.
Because the container might have been damaged since it was loaded.
Because the signal itself might be a fake chalk mark left by an investigator to trap the collector.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: A drop that draws a second glance has already failed, whether or not anyone opens it.
Walking straight from the signal to the drop site creates the very problem the method exists to avoid, because now a follower only has to watch one person do both things back to back.
The container is the first decision.
A good site is public enough that standing there for thirty seconds needs no excuse.

distractorRationale.1: Nothing in the passage says one role is watched more than the other; the risk it names is behavior, not identity, one person doing two connected things in a row.
distractorRationale.2: The passage never raises damage to the container as a reason for caution; that is a worry this article does not mention at all.
distractorRationale.3: The passage never suggests a signal could be faked by an outsider.  Its concern is a follower watching a real signal and a real pickup happen together.

items.explain: The whole method exists to keep two actions from being watched as one.  If the collector skipped their own caution and walked straight to the drop the instant the signal appeared, a follower would only need to watch a single person to prove the whole connection.

items.stem: The article gives real qualities of a good dead-drop location. Choose the three the article actually states.
choices: Close enough to the meeting that the walk takes only minutes
Marked clearly enough that the collector cannot miss it
Busy enough that no one kind of visitor stands out
Public enough that standing there briefly needs no excuse
Guarded enough that a stranger could never reach it
Dull enough that nobody remembers who stood there

distractorRationale.0: The article never talks about distance to a meeting; a dead drop replaces a meeting rather than sitting near one.
distractorRationale.1: A drop that is easy to spot is a drop that has already failed. The whole design depends on nobody but the two sides noticing it at all.
distractorRationale.4: A guarded location is the opposite of what the article recommends. A dead drop needs to look like nowhere in particular, not somewhere protected.

items.explain: A good site is defined by three qualities working together: it is ordinary enough to need no excuse, forgettable enough that nobody remembers standing there, and general enough that no single kind of visitor stands out. Distance, guards, and visibility are never part of the article's own definition.

partA.stem: The article says a repeated scramble "leaves a seam where the repeat shows." What does "seam" mean here?
choices: A physical stitch sewn into the paper the pad is printed on.
A place where a hidden pattern becomes visible to someone looking for it.
A second, identical copy of the pad, kept by the receiver in case the first is lost.
The exact moment the sender finishes combining the message with the pad and sends it.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: A pad is a long string of letters or numbers, chosen at random.
A codebreaker goes looking for that seam first.
Both the sender and the receiver hold an identical copy before anything is sent.
To encode a message, the sender combines it with the pad one character at a time.

distractorRationale.0: The article never mentions paper or stitching. A "seam" here is used the way a crack in a wall is used, a figure of speech for a weak spot, not an actual sewn line.
distractorRationale.2: The receiver's identical copy is real, and it is how the message gets read, not a spare kept in case one is lost.  A seam is a flaw in the scrambling itself, not a copy of anything.
distractorRationale.3: Sending a message is an event in time, while a seam is a place where a pattern shows through. The two ideas belong to different parts of the article.

items.explain: A codebreaker "goes looking for that seam first," which only makes sense if a seam is something that can be found and examined: a spot where a repeated pattern becomes visible, not a physical object or a moment in time.

partA.stem: The article explains the one-use rule in paragraph three before explaining, in paragraph four, how real operators broke it. Why build the article in that order?
choices: So a reader understands exactly what the rule protects before seeing how tempting it is to break.
Because the article is arranged by date, and the rule was invented before any operator broke it.
Because paragraph four is less important, so it is placed after the more important paragraph three.
So the reader can skip paragraph three if they already know what a cipher is.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: A courier gets delayed, a message queue backs up, or fresh pages run short.
Reuse is what breaks a one-time pad, and it breaks completely rather than a little.
None of this makes the method practical at real scale.
It was in the fact that no comparison was ever possible.

distractorRationale.1: The article gives no dates anywhere and never claims to be arranged in the order things happened; it is arranged by idea, not by calendar.
distractorRationale.2: Placement in an article is not a ranking of importance, and paragraph four is not treated as a footnote; it is where the article's real-world warning lives.
distractorRationale.3: The paragraphs build on each other rather than standing alone; skipping the rule would leave a reader with no way to understand what paragraph four says was broken.

items.explain: Paragraph three states plainly that reuse breaks the method completely. Only after a reader understands what is at stake does paragraph four's account of real operators reaching for a used page land as a genuine warning rather than a random detail.

partA.stem: The last paragraph says the method is not "practical at real scale." What does that phrase mean as the article uses it?
choices: The method stops protecting a message once the message grows past a certain length.
The method cannot be broken, but it takes too much effort for everyday traffic.
The method was only ever tested on a small number of messages.
The method needs equipment so expensive that most operations cannot afford to buy it.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Printing, distributing, and guarding enough pad for ordinary daily traffic takes more effort than most operations can sustain.
A cipher that cannot be broken is not the same thing as a cipher anyone can afford to use.
Every letter of every message needs its own fresh page of true randomness, and both sides need an identical, unguessable copy of that page before a single word can be sent.
That is why the method survives today mostly for messages that are short, rare, and important enough to be worth the cost.

distractorRationale.0: The article never says the cipher stops working at some length; its strength is described as complete, not limited by size.
distractorRationale.2: Testing and sample size are never mentioned. The article's worry is the ongoing cost of running the method every day, not how much it was tried before.
distractorRationale.3: Cost here means effort and logistics, printing, distributing, and guarding enough pad, not money for equipment, which the article never raises.

items.explain: The article never says the cipher fails; it says keeping it running is too much work for daily use. "Practical at real scale" is about whether an operation can sustain the effort, not about whether the method itself succeeds.

partA.stem: What job does the article's last paragraph do that the paragraphs before it do not?
choices: It repeats the definition of a one-time pad for a reader who skipped ahead.
It turns from why the cipher is strong to why it is hard to use.
It is where the article first tells the reader what a one-time pad is.
It lists every historical operation where the method was ever broken.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: The one-time pad answers that question about as fully as a cipher can.
Traffic from more than one real operation was eventually broken this way, years after it was sent, when an analyst noticed two messages that scrambled just a little too much alike.
None of this makes the method practical at real scale.
A pad is a long string of letters or numbers, chosen at random.

distractorRationale.0: The last paragraph does not restate the definition; it opens a new question about cost that the earlier paragraphs never raise.
distractorRationale.2: The pad is introduced in paragraph two, long before the last paragraph, so this cannot be the last paragraph's job.
distractorRationale.3: The article names one general pattern of failure, not a list of specific historical operations, and that pattern already appeared in paragraph four.

items.explain: Every earlier paragraph argues the cipher is unbeatable when used correctly. The last paragraph turns to a different question entirely, whether an operation can actually keep up the discipline the method demands, which is why it reads as a turn rather than a repeat.

items.stem: The article explains what happens when a page of the pad is used twice. Choose the three true statements.
choices: A computer is required before reuse can ever be exploited
Comparing two such messages cancels out the randomness that protected them
Reuse makes the cipher a little weaker, but it still cannot be broken by anyone
A trained reader can pick the resulting pattern apart by hand
Reuse was mostly a danger for very short messages, where patterns are easy to spot
Two messages scrambled with one stretch of pad can be compared

distractorRationale.0: The article's own example describes an analyst noticing the pattern by comparing messages, with no mention of a computer at all.
distractorRationale.2: The article says reuse breaks the method completely rather than a little.  Calling the cipher a little weaker but still unbreakable is the opposite of what it claims.
distractorRationale.4: Message length is never connected to the danger of reuse anywhere in the article; the danger comes from repeating the pad, not from how short a message is.

items.explain: Reuse is dangerous specifically because it lets two scrambled messages be lined up against each other, and that comparison is what cancels out the randomness and exposes a pattern a person can work through by hand, a complete failure rather than a partial one.

partA.stem: What does Ines actually decide about the second box the archivist brings her without being asked?
choices: She decides that offering more than was asked for could be kindness or a test, so she should be careful rather than careless.
She decides the archivist must be trying to help the exercise a second player is secretly running.
She decides to refuse the second box outright and hand it back to the archivist.
She decides the second box must be empty, since nobody had requested it.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: One of those names is not on any list she was given.

For one long second she runs the math Marchetti trained into her: a stranger offering more than you asked for is either kindness or a test, and the only way to tell them apart is to notice which one makes you careless.
The unclaimed box sits back on its cart, unopened past the first folder.
The Halloway folder is exactly where the request slip said it would be.

distractorRationale.1: That detail is about the request slips she reads earlier, a separate observation from her reasoning about the box itself.
distractorRationale.2: Refusing the box outright is not what the passage shows; she takes both boxes and opens the second one last, carefully, rather than turning it away.
distractorRationale.3: The passage never says or implies the box is empty; it says she opens it slowly and last, which only makes sense if there is something in it to be cautious about.

items.explain: Ines does not panic or refuse the unexpected box. She applies a rule Marchetti trained into her: unearned generosity is either kindness or a trap, and the way to tell them apart is to watch for whichever one makes you careless, then acts on that rule by opening the second box last and slowly.

partA.stem: What does Ines learn from reading the request slips left in the tray while she waits?
choices: That the Halloway folder she came for has already been checked out by somebody else.
That the archivist has been assigned to watch her specifically.
That someone not on her list asked for boxes from her shelf range this month.
That the archive closes earlier than the fifteen minutes she was told to wait.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: He asks what she is researching, in the bored voice of someone who asks it forty times a day.
One of those names is not on any list she was given.
He slides a slip across the counter, telling her the boxes take fifteen minutes to bring up from the stacks.
The Halloway folder is exactly where the request slip said it would be.

distractorRationale.0: That sentence says the folder turns up exactly where it was expected, which is the opposite of already checked out by somebody else.
distractorRationale.1: That line describes the archivist's manner toward every visitor, not information Ines gathers about the case from the slips.
distractorRationale.3: The fifteen minutes is stated as the normal wait time, not a closing time, and it is what gives her the chance to read the slips in the first place.

items.explain: Ines uses her waiting time to read the request slips upside down, and what she finds is a name on the same shelf range that was never on the list Marchetti gave her, a detail that raises a question the passage leaves open rather than answers.

partA.stem: Why does the narrator hold off calling Marchetti at two-twenty-five, even though Ines is already late checking in?
choices: Because Ines had already sent a text that the narrator simply had not noticed yet.
Because the narrator cannot reach Marchetti's contact from inside the parked car.
Because the plan has a margin on purpose, and late is not the same as gone.
Because the narrator's job is to write the times down, not to make the call.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: My phone sits face up on the dashboard so I do not have to pick it up to see the screen.
At two-twenty-seven the phone buzzes once.
A plan has a margin built into it on purpose, and using the margin is not the same as the plan failing.
I write down the time anyway.

distractorRationale.0: The passage never suggests a missed text; the narrator has heard nothing at all by two-twenty-five, and that silence is exactly the problem being weighed.
distractorRationale.1: The phone sitting face up is about how closely the narrator is watching the screen, not about whether a call is physically possible to make.
distractorRationale.3: The plan says that if nothing has come by two-twenty-five, the narrator calls Marchetti, so making that call is part of the job.  Writing the time down is something the narrator does as well, not instead.

items.explain: The narrator reasons from a rule Ines herself explained earlier: a plan's built-in margin exists so a few late minutes do not automatically mean disaster. Two-twenty-five is late by the plan's own clock, but the narrator treats late and gone as two different facts rather than collapsing them into one.

partA.stem: This scene is told in first person, from the watcher's own point of view.  What does that choice let the reader experience that a third-person account of the same events would not?
choices: The narrator's own uncertainty in the moment, including a decision not made, not only how the wait ends.
A clear view into what is happening inside the archive while the narrator waits outside.
A complete, timed list of everyone who enters and exits the archive building during the wait.
Proof of exactly what Ines is thinking while she is inside.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: At two-twenty-one the same man walks back out, alone, checking his phone the way people do when they are actually checking their phone and not pretending to.
My thumb hovers over Marchetti's contact, and I do not press it.
Ines gave me the reason once herself, after her own turn watching a door.
At two-nineteen a man in a grey jacket walks in through the archive doors.

distractorRationale.1: The narrator sees the doors from outside, but nothing here shows what is happening inside the archive; the viewpoint stays limited to the parking lot throughout.
distractorRationale.2: One man entering and leaving is a single observation, not a complete record of everyone who came and went; the passage never claims to track every visitor.
distractorRationale.3: This line explains a rule Ines shared at some earlier point, not a window into what she is thinking during this specific wait.

items.explain: A third-person, outside account could report only that the narrator waited and then received a signal.  Writing it in first person instead lets the reader sit inside the narrator's own held breath and the thumb that hovers but does not press, an uncertainty a purely external account would have to leave out.

items.stem: The passage names specific things Ines actually notices during the exercise. Choose the three the passage actually states.
choices: A lanyard on the archivist that says TRAINEE
A second name on the shelf request slips that was not on her own list
A note left inside the Halloway folder addressed to her
A security camera pointed at the reading room table
A second box the archivist brings her without being asked
An exit that the archivist tells her is reserved for staff only

distractorRationale.2: The Halloway folder contains photographs and a page of notes, not any note addressed to Ines personally.
distractorRationale.3: No camera is ever mentioned in the passage; nothing in the scene describes how the room is watched.
distractorRationale.5: The passage never describes a staff-only exit or any instruction about how she is meant to leave.

items.explain: Three concrete details anchor this scene: the trainee lanyard, the unfamiliar name on the shelf slips, and the unrequested second box. Every other option invents a detail, a camera, a personal note, a restricted exit, that this passage never actually gives.

partA.stem: The brief's small print says the thirty-day figure was measured at a constant seventy degrees.  Why should that detail make a reader slow down before trusting the number?
choices: Because the headline number describes one comfortable condition, not every condition a buyer might use the tag in.
Because seventy degrees is an unusually high temperature for any lab to use in a battery test.
Because it proves the thirty-day figure was invented by the sellers rather than measured in a test.
Because it means the tag cannot function at any other temperature.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the brief best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: It states that the thirty-day figure was measured at a constant seventy degrees, and that battery performance in other conditions may vary.
The Petrel-4 is rated for water, dust, and a two-meter drop onto concrete.
Our engineers ran that test at our own facility, cycling the unit through a normal daily routine of movement and stillness for the entire month.
Contact our sales office to arrange a live demonstration at your own site, and ask about volume pricing for departments ordering more than ten units.

distractorRationale.1: Seventy degrees is a comfortable, ordinary room temperature, not an unusually high one; the brief itself calls it constant rather than extreme.
distractorRationale.2: The brief does not say the number was invented; it says the number was measured under one specific condition, which is a different and much narrower claim.
distractorRationale.3: "Performance may vary" concedes the tag still works elsewhere, just not necessarily for as long; it does not claim the tag stops functioning outside seventy degrees.

items.explain: A number that holds true at one comfortable temperature is not automatically true everywhere else.  The brief's own small print admits performance may vary, which is exactly the kind of detail a careful reader has to notice before assuming the headline claim applies to their own conditions.

partA.stem: According to the training log, what does bringing the dead tags back indoors and warming them up show?
choices: That the tree cover at the test site had no effect on the results.
That warming the tags settled which of the staff's two guesses about the cause was right.
That the cold did not damage the tags, since they all came back to life once warm.
That the maker's thirty-day figure was measured indoors rather than outdoors.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the log best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Each tag was brought in and warmed up before staff checked it again, and all four came back to life within minutes.
The staff have two guesses.
The tag may also have searched harder for a signal in a test site with more tree cover than the maker used.
This entry will be checked again after a planned trial in February, at a colder site.

distractorRationale.0: Tree cover is offered as one of the staff's two guesses about the cause, not something the recovery test ruled in or out.
distractorRationale.1: The staff's two guesses come after the warming, and the log says neither guess was tested this time.  Warming the tags shows only that the cold did no lasting damage.
distractorRationale.3: The log never says where the maker's own test was run; it only reports where the Halloway trial took place.

items.explain: Warming the tags and watching all four come back within minutes tells the staff the cold had not broken anything permanently. That single result rules out damage as the explanation and points toward something about cold temperature itself draining the charge.
