partA.stem: How does the training log itself signal that its explanation for the short battery life is not yet proven?
choices: It says the times were lost, so the test must be run again in February.
It says the trip was only a test of whether the tags could replace the older trackers.
It calls its two explanations guesses and says neither was tested this time.
It says the two trainers who signed it, Osei and Marchetti, disagreed about the cause.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the log best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Neither guess was tested this time, so both stay questions for the next trial rather than settled facts.
It is dated the second of January and signed by two trainers, Osei and Marchetti.
Four Petrel-4 tags went out on the January cold-weather trip, to test whether they could replace the site's older trackers for winter work.
This entry will be checked again after a planned trial in February, at a colder site.

distractorRationale.0: The times were not lost.  The log records that two tags went silent about sixty hours in and that the longest stopped just past sixty-eight hours.  The February trial is planned so the entry can be checked again at a colder site.
distractorRationale.1: That is the trip's purpose, stated in the opening line.  It tells you why the tags went out, not how sure the staff are about why they went silent.
distractorRationale.3: Two names signing an entry shows who is responsible for it.  Nothing in the log says Osei and Marchetti disagreed, and it gives its two guesses side by side.

items.explain: A source that calls its own explanation a guess and names it as untested is being honest about the limits of what it has shown. That single admission is what separates a careful field log from a source that overstates what one trial can actually prove.

partA.stem: Why does the log say a tag rated for thirty days that only lasts three in the cold "is not broken"?
choices: Because the published number describes one set of conditions, and a Halloway winter is a different set.
Because three days is actually longer than the staff expected the tag to last in that cold.
Because the tag was built for use indoors and was never designed to go outdoors at all.
Because a faulty tag would not have come back to life once warmed.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the log best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: That holds true until someone measures a real cold-weather number, instead of assuming the summer number still applies.
It is a tag whose one published number describes one set of conditions, and a Halloway winter is not that set.
The trip ran across three days.
Each tag was brought in and warmed up before staff checked it again, and all four came back to life within minutes.

distractorRationale.1: The log treats three days as a serious shortfall worth investigating, not as an outcome it expected or welcomed.
distractorRationale.2: Nothing in the log or the brief says the tag is indoor-only; the whole exercise is an outdoor cold-weather trial.
distractorRationale.3: The recovery detail supports a different point, that the cold did not damage the tags, which is related but answers a different question than whether the tag is faulty.

items.explain: A published number is a description of the conditions it was measured under, not a promise that holds everywhere.  Calling the tag not broken separates a real defect from a number that simply describes a different, warmer set of conditions than the one it was carried into.

items.stem: The brief gives a reader several real reasons to be cautious about its thirty-day claim. Choose the three the brief actually supports.
choices: The engineers who ran the test work for the company that sells the tag
The brief refuses to say how the battery is charged
The small print admits performance may vary outside the tested condition
The brief admits the thirty-day figure was never actually reached in testing
The housing colors described in the brief do not match the photograph
The brief carries no date, so a reader cannot tell how current the claim is

distractorRationale.1: The brief states plainly that the tag charges from any standard cable in under two hours; charging is not withheld information.
distractorRationale.3: The brief says the tag held a working fix for the full thirty days every time; it never admits the figure was missed.
distractorRationale.4: The brief mentions housing colors but describes no photograph at all, so there is nothing for a color to mismatch.

items.explain: A careful reader watches for exactly these three signals: who ran the test, whether the claim can be dated and checked against anything else, and whether the source itself admits a limit. The brief supplies all three, which is why its headline number deserves a second look rather than outright trust.

partA.stem: The tunnel report in this level states each of its causes as plain fact.  Which sentence in this tag article gives its cause more cautiously?
choices: The cold sentence, which says freezing air drains a battery's charge
The desert sentence, which says hot stretches seemed to wear the battery down
The mild-weather sentence, which says mild weather costs the least
The mountain sentence, which says the board called that runtime far below the rest

partB.stem: Which sentence from the article best supports your answer?
choices: Cold is the clearest of the three factors.
Mild weather costs the least of the three, which is why a maker's own test, run at a comfortable room temperature, tends to show the best number the device can reach.
A tag there lasted just under three days before it went silent, a runtime the board called far below every other test.
That tag lasted only nineteen days, as repeated hot stretches seemed to wear the battery down faster than a mild day would.

distractorRationale.0: The cold sentence is stated flatly, and calling cold the clearest of the three factors is a confident claim, not a cautious one.
distractorRationale.2: Mild weather costing the least is stated as plain fact, and the sentence goes on to explain the maker's number with it.
distractorRationale.3: That sentence reports a runtime and what the board called it.  It names no cause, so there is nothing in it to hedge.

items.explain: Setting two sources side by side includes noticing how sure each one is.  The tunnel report states its causes plainly, and most of this article does too, but the desert sentence says the hot stretches seemed to wear the battery down, which presents the cause as a likely reading of the result rather than a measured fact.

partA.stem: Read together rather than one at a time, what do the article's three test results actually prove about the tag?
choices: That only the coastal result should be trusted, since it is closest to the maker's claim.
That the tag is unreliable and should not be trusted in any climate.
That the desert test was performed incorrectly, since heat should not affect a battery.
That the tag itself did not change between tests; the climate it was tested in did.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the article best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Read together, the three results say something more exact.
A buyer who reads only the top line could easily call the tag bad, or great, depending on which single test they saw.
The tag did not change between tests.  The climate did.
That is close to the maker's own thirty-day number, and a range a buyer could plan around.

distractorRationale.0: Trusting only the closest-to-claim result is the same mistake in the opposite direction, cherry-picking one number instead of reading all three together.
distractorRationale.1: The article argues against exactly this reading; calling the tag simply unreliable is the mistake a reader makes by trusting only one test in isolation.
distractorRationale.2: The article never questions whether the desert test was performed correctly; it treats heat as a real, expected factor in battery performance, not an error.

items.explain: A single test result can look like a verdict on the device. Placing all three side by side changes the conclusion entirely: the one thing that stayed constant was the tag, and the one thing that changed each time was the climate around it.

partA.stem: Which piece of advice does this article's own evidence actually support?
choices: Use a tracking tag only in mild weather, since mild weather costs the least runtime.
Keep tags out of the heat, since heat drains a battery faster than the cold does.
Ask what temperature a number was measured at, since it describes one climate.
Leave the tag at home on cold trips, since in freezing air it lasts under three days.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the article best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Two numbers measured in two different climates are not really being compared at all.
Mild weather costs the least of the three, which is why a maker's own test, run at a comfortable room temperature, tends to show the best number the device can reach.
That tag lasted only nineteen days, as repeated hot stretches seemed to wear the battery down faster than a mild day would.
A tag there lasted just under three days before it went silent, a runtime the board called far below every other test.

distractorRationale.0: Mild weather does cost the least, and the article never tells a buyer to stay out of every other climate.  It says to ask for the right number, not to stop using the tag.
distractorRationale.1: Heat does cost the tag runtime, nineteen days against twenty-six, and the freezing test cost far more, just under three days.  Advice that ranks heat as the worst climate gets the article's own numbers backwards.
distractorRationale.3: Just under three days is one test's result in one freezing climate.  The article's advice is to ask for the cold number before you plan, not to stop carrying the tag.

items.explain: The article's central argument is that a runtime number only means something once its conditions are known. The advice that follows directly from that evidence is to ask what temperature a figure was measured at, not to trust a single number or avoid a climate outright.

partA.stem: What does the board's evidence show about the tag in mild weather?
choices: It ran longer than the maker's own number had promised
It ran out sooner than it did in the desert heat
It gave the shortest runtime the board recorded
It ran close to the maker's own thirty-day number

partB.stem: Which sentence from the article best supports your answer?
choices: A tag there lasted just under three days before it went silent, a runtime the board called far below every other test.
That is close to the maker's own thirty-day number, and a range a buyer could plan around.
A tag there ran for twenty-six days on one charge.
That tag lasted only nineteen days, as repeated hot stretches seemed to wear the battery down faster than a mild day would.

distractorRationale.0: Twenty-six days is short of the maker's thirty, not longer.  Reading a big number as a win skips the comparison the board makes.
distractorRationale.1: The desert tag lasted nineteen days, so the mild tag outlasted it by a week.
distractorRationale.2: The shortest runtime was the mountain test, just under three days.  Mild weather gave the longest runtime of the three.

items.explain: The board puts its mild-weather result in context with a single sentence:  twenty-six days is close to the maker's own thirty-day number, and a range a buyer could plan around.  That sentence is the evidence for what mild weather showed, in that one climate.

items.stem: The tunnel report in this level says its three conditions are properties of the ground, not of the beacon.  Choose the two statements that show this tag article treating the weather the same way, as the cause rather than the tag.
choices: It says the tag that went silent in the mountains was a faulty unit
It says heat costs runtime too, wearing a battery down over hot stretches
It ranks the tag against other brands tested in the same three climates
It says mild weather costs a battery the least of the three conditions
It says the mountain runtime was far below the other two tests

distractorRationale.0: The article blames the cold for the mountain result.  Nothing in it says the unit was faulty.
distractorRationale.2: Only one tag was tested.  The article compares climates, not brands, so it has nothing to rank.
distractorRationale.4: That compares one result with the others.  It does not say what caused the short runtime.

items.explain: The tunnel report pins its results on the ground rather than the beacon, and this article does the same with the weather.  Heat costs runtime in its own way, over repeated hot stretches, and mild weather costs the least, so each result is a reading of its weather rather than a mark against the tag.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that each give a real example, rather than stating a general rule.
spans: A hollow bolt can thread into a fence post, a magnetic box can hide under a mailbox lip, or a folded paper can wait behind a loose brick.
Instead the two sides agree on a signal placed somewhere else: a chalk mark on a lamppost, a strip of tape on a stop sign, or a plant moved from one side of a window to the other.
The container is the first decision.
The collector cannot walk past the site every day just to check, because repetition is its own kind of pattern.
A drop that draws a second glance has already failed, whether or not anyone opens it.
items.explain: Two sentences give concrete examples, specific hiding spots and specific signals. The rest state general rules the article wants a reader to remember, not particular instances of them.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that state the article's overall point, rather than describing one single step in the method.
spans: That is the whole point of splitting a handoff into two halves separated by hours or days instead of by feet.
Nobody has to be caught in the same place at the same time as anybody else, and a connection nobody observed can never later be proven.
The location matters as much as the container.
A park bench works.
Empty hands are never the failure.
items.explain: The article's two closing sentences state why the whole method exists: splitting a handoff so nobody is ever caught together. The other sentences describe one piece of how that gets done, not why it matters.

items.stem: Finish the summary.  A dead drop works because {{0}}, and the collector still moves carefully at pickup because {{1}}.

choices: the two sides never have to be in one place at one time
the person who loads it waits nearby to watch the pickup
the signal is broadcast on the radio for anyone nearby to hear
the container might not be waterproof, so rain could ruin whatever is hidden inside
a follower watching the signal could trail whoever checks it straight to the drop
a chalk mark fades so fast that the collector could miss the signal altogether

items.explain: The method works because it removes the moment when two people would be in the same place at once.  The collector still moves carefully because walking straight from the signal to the drop would let a follower see one person check the signal and then go to the drop, which is the link the method exists to hide.

items.stem: Tap the sentence that defines what a one-time pad IS, and the sentence that explains what makes it unbreakable.  Two of these sentences do something else.
spans: A pad is a long string of letters or numbers, chosen at random.
Without the pad, every possible original message is equally likely to be hiding inside it.
A codebreaker goes looking for that seam first.
Historically, this single rule is the one real operators broke under pressure, not the math behind it.
items.explain: One sentence defines what a pad physically is, a random string of characters, and the other explains the exact property that makes it unbreakable, that no possible original message is favored over any other. The rest describe codebreakers and history rather than defining anything.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that each open a new paragraph's main idea.  Two of these sentences come from inside a paragraph instead.
spans: The one-time pad answers that question about as fully as a cipher can.
None of this makes the method practical at real scale.
The rule for combining them is fixed, and anyone could learn it in a minute.
Two messages scrambled with the same stretch of pad can be compared against each other.
items.explain: Each paragraph in this article opens with a sentence that announces its own job. The two chosen here open the paragraph about what the pad is and the paragraph about why it is hard to use, while the other two are supporting detail from the middle of a paragraph.

items.stem: Finish the summary.  A one-time pad stays unbreakable only if {{0}}, because reusing a page lets two messages be {{1}}.

choices: the pad is printed on paper that no water can damage
each page is used exactly once, then destroyed
the message is written in numbers instead of letters
traced back to the courier who first carried them
sent over a faster radio frequency that a listener can catch
compared against each other, which cancels the randomness out

items.explain: The pad's strength depends entirely on the one-use rule, not on the material it is printed on or the frequency a message travels over.  Reuse matters because it lets two scrambled messages be lined up against each other, and that comparison is what cancels out the randomness that was protecting them.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that show Ines being deliberately cautious, rather than simply going along with what happens.
spans: For one long second she runs the math Marchetti trained into her: a stranger offering more than you asked for is either kindness or a test, and the only way to tell them apart is to notice which one makes you careless.
The second box she opens last, and slowly, turning each folder over before she reads it, the way you check a step before you put your weight on it.
She thanks him, takes both boxes to the table nearest the window, and opens the one she actually came for first.
He wears a lanyard that says TRAINEE, and a stack of request slips he clearly has not finished sorting.
items.explain: Two moments show Ines actively deciding to be careful: reasoning through what the second box might mean, and physically opening it last and slowly. Taking the boxes to the table and describing the archivist's lanyard are ordinary narration, not choices Ines is making on purpose.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that show the narrator separating what was actually observed from what was only guessed.
spans: Marchetti's other rule is that you log what you saw, not what you decided it meant.
Deciding what a stranger in a jacket was doing is exactly the kind of decision that has burned people before me.
At two-nineteen a man in a grey jacket walks in through the archive doors.
My phone sits face up on the dashboard so I do not have to pick it up to see the screen.
items.explain: The narrator states the rule directly, log what you saw, not what you decided it meant, and then explains why guessing at a stranger's reason is dangerous. The other two sentences are plain observations, not the narrator reflecting on the difference between seeing and assuming.

items.stem: Finish the summary.  Ines treats the unclaimed second box with caution because {{0}}, and she signs the log honestly at the end because {{1}}.

choices: a stranger offering more than was asked for could be a trap as easily as kindness
the archivist warned her that the second box from that shelf was dangerous
Marchetti had warned her specifically about that shelf before she went in
a reading room keeps that record whether she lies or not
she forgot to bring the false name Marchetti gave her
the archivist was watching closely as she signed it

items.explain: Ines's caution comes from a rule, not a specific warning: an unearned offer could be a trap as easily as kindness.  Her honest signature comes from the same clear-eyed reasoning, since a reading room keeps its record regardless of what name goes on it, so a lie buys nothing unless somebody happens to be checking.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences from the brief that a careful reader should treat as a claim needing a check, rather than a plain, checkable fact.
spans: Not once during the full thirty days did the tag miss a scheduled report.
No other tag in its size class has matched that number under comparable conditions.
It charges from any standard cable in under two hours and pairs with a phone app in seconds.
The housing comes in three colors, though the electronics inside are identical across all three.
items.explain: A perfect thirty-day record and a claim of beating every competitor are both performance claims made by the seller, with no outside source to check them against. Charging time and housing colors are plain, easily verified specifications, not the kind of claim that needs a second opinion.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that report a measured result, rather than the staff's explanation for it.
spans: By the end of day two, two of the four tags had gone silent, about sixty hours into what the brief calls a thirty-day battery life.
The longest one stopped just past sixty-eight hours.
A cold battery cannot give its full stored charge, and that is true of batteries in general, not just this tag.
The tag may also have searched harder for a signal in a test site with more tree cover than the maker used.
items.explain: The two chosen sentences report exact times the staff observed and wrote down. The other two are the staff's own guesses about what caused those times, explicitly labeled elsewhere in the log as untested explanations rather than measurements.

items.stem: Finish the summary.  The Petrel-4 brief's thirty-day claim deserves caution because {{0}}, while the Halloway log's shorter number deserves more trust because {{1}}.

choices: the engineers who ran the test work for the company that sells the tag
a tag the size of a matchbook is too small to hold a real battery
the brief's thirty-day number was never measured by anyone at all
it names its dates and conditions and admits its explanation is still just a guess
it was written by Corvid Systems, the same company that sells the tag
it promises the tag will run even longer than the brief's thirty days

items.explain: The brief's number is worth a second look because the people who measured it are the people who sell the product.  The log earns more trust for the opposite reason: it names exactly when and under what conditions it tested, and it is honest that its own explanation has not yet been proven.  The brief's number was measured, by Corvid's own engineers at Corvid's own facility, and nothing says the tag is too small for a real battery.  The log was written by the Halloway staff rather than Corvid, and its number is shorter than thirty days, not longer.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that state the article's central lesson about reading a single test result.  Two of these sentences report one specific test instead.
spans: Read alone, each number looks like a verdict on the tag itself.
The tag did not change between tests.
A tag there ran for twenty-six days on one charge.
That tag lasted only nineteen days, as repeated hot stretches seemed to wear the battery down faster than a mild day would.
items.explain: The article's lesson is that a single number can be mistaken for a verdict on the device, when really the tag never changed and only the climate did. The other two sentences report exactly the kind of single test result the lesson is warning a reader not to over-trust.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that give practical advice to a buyer, rather than reporting what one test found.
spans: Ask what temperature a number was measured at before you compare it to any other number.
It means a number describes one climate, not every climate, and a buyer who needs the cold to work has to ask for the cold number rather than accept the warmest one on offer.
The third test ran in a freezing mountain climate.
A tag there ran for twenty-six days on one charge.
items.explain: Two sentences tell a buyer what to actually do: ask for the temperature behind a number, and demand the cold figure rather than settle for the warmest one offered. The other two simply report what happened in one specific test, without telling a reader what to do about it.

items.stem: Finish the summary.  Reading all three climate tests together shows that {{0}}, so a careful buyer should {{1}}.

choices: the tag itself never changed between tests, only the climate around it did
the desert test must have used a broken tag that drained too early
only the mild coastal number, near thirty days, can be trusted
ask what temperature any runtime number was measured at before comparing it to another
buy only tags tested in mild coastal climates, where the runtime ran longest
ignore every runtime number a maker publishes, since the three tests disagree

items.explain: Three results, read side by side, isolate the one thing that actually varied: the climate around a tag that itself never changed.  The advice that follows is to ask what conditions any single number was measured under.

items.stem: According to the article, what happens to a container that draws a second glance from a stranger?
choices: It has already failed as a drop, whether or not the stranger opens it.
It is immediately reported to an investigator by the stranger.
It is replaced with a different container at the same site the next day.
It still succeeds as long as the stranger does not open it.

distractorRationale.1: The article never claims a stranger reports anything; it only says the drop has already failed once it draws a second look.
distractorRationale.2: The article never describes replacing a container the next day; a failed drop is not given a second chance in the text.
distractorRationale.3: The article says failure happens the moment a second glance is drawn, regardless of whether the container is ever opened. Not opening it does not undo that failure.

items.explain: A drop's success depends entirely on going unnoticed. The instant it draws a second glance, the article calls it already failed, whether or not the stranger ever opens it, because being noticed is the actual danger, not being opened.

items.stem: Which choice best states why the article says a dead drop takes the second person out of the picture?
choices: It removes the moment two people would stand together, the only proof a follower could use to connect them.
Only one person is ever trained to both load and collect drops, so a second person has no job.
A second person would make the container too heavy to hide.
The collector always works completely alone, without any trainer to show them where the drop is.

distractorRationale.1: The article never claims only one person is trained; it describes two roles, loading and collecting, without saying either is done by an untrained person.
distractorRationale.2: Container weight is never mentioned as a concern connected to a second person.
distractorRationale.3: The article never says who trains the collector or what a trainer shows them.  It takes the second person out so that no follower ever sees two people in one place at one time.

items.explain: A meeting proves a connection because a follower can see two people together at once.  Removing the second person from that single moment removes the only proof a follower would have, which is the entire reason the method works.

items.stem: Why does the article say a place only one kind of person would visit never works as a drop site?
choices: Such a place is usually too small or too crowded to hide a container in safely.
An investigator would ask first about the one reason anyone is there.
Such a place is too far from where the meeting would be, so the walk takes too long.
A follower could not reach such a place without being seen, which would give the drop away.

distractorRationale.0: The article never gives size or crowding as a reason a site fails.  It gives one reason, and that reason is about who would be there.
distractorRationale.2: Distance from a meeting is irrelevant here; a dead drop replaces a meeting rather than sitting near one.
distractorRationale.3: The article's concern is what an investigator would ask about a visitor's reason for being there, not whether a follower could physically reach the spot.

items.explain: A site that only one kind of person visits gives an investigator a single, obvious question to ask about anyone seen there. A good site avoids that question entirely by being ordinary enough that nobody needs an excuse to be there.

items.stem: Match each part of the method to the specific risk the article says it protects against.
rowLabels: Building the container to look ordinary
Choosing a public, forgettable location
Placing the signal somewhere other than the drop site
colLabels: A stranger giving the container a second glance
An investigator having one obvious question to ask about a visitor
The collector creating a noticeable pattern by checking daily
items.explain: Each part of the method solves one specific risk. The container's disguise stops a stranger's glance, a forgettable public location stops an investigator's obvious question, and moving the check to a separate signal stops the collector from creating a visitable pattern.

items.stem: What does the article mean by calling a properly used one-time pad "closer to a lock with no shape for a key to have ever fit"?
choices: Without the pad, every possible original message is equally likely, so a codebreaker has nothing to unlock.
The one-time pad was invented by a locksmith, which is why the article calls it a lock.
The rule for combining the pad with a message is kept secret, so no codebreaker can learn it.
The pad can be used to unlock a message once, but never a second time.

distractorRationale.1: The article never discusses who invented the one-time pad or what profession they had.
distractorRationale.2: The article says the opposite about the rule: it is fixed, and anyone could learn it in a minute.  The protection comes from the random pad, not from a secret rule.
distractorRationale.3: The "no shape for a key" image describes the scrambled message itself being unopenable, not a limit on how many times the pad can be used.

items.explain: A lock with no shape for a key to fit cannot be picked, because there is nothing about it a key could match.  The article uses that image to explain that a properly used one-time pad leaves no pattern at all for a codebreaker to work against.

items.stem: Why does the article explain what a one-time pad is before explaining the rule that makes it work?
choices: The one-use rule was discovered first, and the pad itself was invented after it.
The one-use rule makes sense only once you know what gets combined with what.
The article is arranged from the least important idea to the most important idea.
The definition paragraph is the shortest one, so it is the easiest to read first.

distractorRationale.0: The article gives no dates and never claims the rule predates the invention; it presents ideas in a logical order, not a historical one.
distractorRationale.2: Paragraph order is not a ranking of importance in this article; each paragraph builds on the one before it.
distractorRationale.3: The definition paragraph is the longest one in the article, not the shortest.  Paragraph length is never a reason the article gives for its order, and each paragraph builds on the one before it.

items.explain: Explaining that a pad combines with a message one character at a time gives a reader the mechanism they need before the next paragraph can explain why using each stretch only once matters. Skipping the definition would leave the rule floating without anything to attach to.

items.stem: In the article, what does an operator "reaching for a page already used" mean?
choices: Turning to an old, worn-out paper notebook instead of opening a fresh one.
Reusing a stretch of pad that already scrambled an earlier message.
Asking a different operator to send the same message out a second time.
Writing a message in pencil instead of ink.

distractorRationale.0: The article never distinguishes new notebooks from worn ones; its concern is whether a specific stretch of the pad has been used before, not the notebook's condition.
distractorRationale.2: The article describes one operator reusing pad material under pressure, not two operators sending duplicate messages.
distractorRationale.3: Pencil versus ink is never mentioned anywhere in the article; the danger is reusing random material, not the writing instrument.

items.explain: The article's whole warning centers on one specific mistake: using a stretch of the pad a second time instead of destroying it after one use. That reuse, not the age of a notebook or the tool used to write, is what breaks the cipher.

items.stem: Put the ideas of the article in the order they appear.
tiles: Real operators who broke the one-use rule under pressure
What a one-time pad is and why it cannot be broken when used correctly
Why the method is too costly to use for ordinary daily traffic
Why any repeated scrambling pattern can eventually be broken
The one rule that makes the method work, and what breaks it
items.explain: The article moves from the general weakness every cipher risks, to what a one-time pad is, to the single rule that makes it unbreakable, to real operators who broke that rule, and finally to why keeping the rule is too costly for everyday use. Each idea sets up the one that follows it.

items.stem: What does Ines find when she reads the request slips left in the tray?
choices: A password she would need before the archivist could bring up the Halloway folder
A note from Marchetti warning her that a second player has joined the exercise
Someone not on her list who asked for boxes from her shelf range
A different address for the county archive, written on the back of a slip

distractorRationale.0: The passage never mentions a password; the folder is retrieved normally through the archivist and photographed.
distractorRationale.1: No note from Marchetti appears anywhere in the passage; the second name is something Ines herself notices and has to interpret.
distractorRationale.3: No alternate address appears in the passage; Ines is already inside the correct archive.

items.explain: The request slips give Ines one specific, unexplained fact: a name on the same shelf range that Marchetti never gave her.  Noticing a detail that does not fit the plan is exactly the habit this exercise trains.

items.stem: What does the narrator do differently from simply reacting to whatever is seen through the windshield?
choices: The narrator calls Marchetti the instant anything outside the windshield looks unusual.
The narrator leaves the car to get a closer look at the man in the grey jacket.
The narrator logs only what was seen, and not what it might have meant.
The narrator ignores the two-twenty-five deadline and waits for Ines no matter what.

distractorRationale.0: The narrator specifically does not call the moment something looks unusual, choosing instead to wait inside the plan's built-in margin.
distractorRationale.1: The passage never shows the narrator leaving the car; every observation happens from the parked vantage point.
distractorRationale.3: The deadline is not ignored.  The narrator's thumb hovers over Marchetti's contact at two-twenty-five, and the wait that follows stays inside the plan's margin, not a wait with no end.

items.explain: Rather than acting on every passing impression, the narrator follows Marchetti's rule of logging what was seen and setting aside any guess about what it meant, which is what lets a stranger in a jacket pass by without triggering an early call.

items.stem: The Reading Room and On the Line both follow a character making a careful decision under pressure.  What is different about how each scene lets the reader experience that decision?
choices: One is told from outside the decision-maker in third person, and the other from inside, in first person.
One takes place during the day in the archive, and the other takes place entirely at night.
One character is nervous about the plan, and the other gets through the whole task feeling no pressure.
One scene includes dialogue, and the other scene includes none at all.

distractorRationale.1: Neither passage specifies day or night as a point of contrast; nothing in either text supports a claim about lighting or time.
distractorRationale.2: Both characters register pressure in their own way; the narrator of the watching scene notices a held breath, and Ines runs through careful reasoning of her own.
distractorRationale.3: The Reading Room includes brief dialogue with the archivist, and On the Line includes almost none, but that is not the deeper contrast the question is asking about.

items.explain: The Reading Room is told about Ines from outside, so the reader watches her actions and infers her reasoning.  On the Line is narrated by the watcher directly, so the reader sits inside a held breath and a thumb that hovers but does not press, an intimacy that third person does not offer in the same way.

items.stem: In four words or fewer, what does Ines do with the second box before she ever opens it?
items.explain: Ines takes both boxes but treats them differently: the one she came for gets opened first, and the unexpected second box is opened last, slowly, the same caution she would use checking a step before trusting her weight to it.

items.stem: A department is deciding whether to trust the Petrel-4 for a winter mission next month. The brief promises thirty days and the Halloway log measured about three in the cold. Which source should the department plan around?
choices: The brief, because it was written by the engineers who designed and built the tag.
The brief, because thirty days is the safer number to plan a mission around.
Neither, because two sources that disagree this much simply cancel each other out.
The log, because it measured the tag in the cold the mission will face.

distractorRationale.0: The engineers who designed the tag also sell it, which is precisely the detail that should make their own number less automatically trustworthy, not more.
distractorRationale.1: Planning around the bigger number is the riskier choice, not the safer one; a team expecting thirty days and losing power at three is stranded exactly when the plan says everything is fine.
distractorRationale.2: Two disagreeing sources are a reason to examine how each was measured, not a reason to abandon the question; one names its dates and conditions and the other does not.

items.explain: Both sources describe the same tag, but only one was measured under the winter conditions the department is actually planning for. That match between the log's test conditions and the department's real mission is what makes it the safer number to plan around, not who wrote it or which number is bigger.

items.stem: Why does the training log describe its own explanation for the short battery life as a "guess" rather than stating it as settled fact?
choices: The staff tested whether the tags recovered, not what caused the charge loss, so the cause is unconfirmed.
The two trainers could not agree on which of their two guesses belonged in the entry.
The maker's brief had already explained the cold drain, and the log trusted that instead.
The tags were too damaged afterward to be examined again.

distractorRationale.1: Both instructors sign the same entry together; nothing in the log suggests disagreement between them.
distractorRationale.2: The brief offers no cold-weather explanation at all; it only claims a thirty-day figure measured at seventy degrees.
distractorRationale.3: The tags are shown recovering fully once warmed, which is the opposite of being too damaged to examine.

items.explain: The staff tested whether the cold had permanently damaged the tags, and it had not, but that same test does not prove what actually caused the fast charge loss in the first place.  Calling the explanation a guess is the log being precise about which question its evidence actually answers.

items.stem: What makes the Halloway log a more careful source than the Petrel-4 brief, based on the details each one includes?
choices: The log tested the tags at Corvid's own facility, where the brief's test was run.
The log runs much longer than the brief, with more paragraphs and longer sentences.
The log names its dates, temperatures and signers, and admits what is unproven.
The log gives just one runtime for all four tags, while the brief gives several.

distractorRationale.0: The log's tags went out on a three-day cold-weather trip, not to Corvid's facility.  Only the brief's own test was run at the company's facility.
distractorRationale.1: Length is not what the passage points to as a mark of care; a long document can still hide its testing conditions, and a short one can state them plainly.
distractorRationale.3: It is the other way round.  The log reports several times, about sixty hours for two tags and just past sixty-eight hours for the longest, while the brief gives the one number thirty days.

items.explain: Care in a source shows up in what it is willing to name and what it refuses to claim. The log states its dates, its temperatures, its instructors, and flags its own explanation as unproven, while the brief offers one favorable number with far less about how it was produced.

items.stem: Match each weakness in the Petrel-4 brief to what that weakness costs a reader.
rowLabels: No date anywhere on the brief
The test was run by the company's own engineers
The thirty-day figure names only one temperature
colLabels: The number cannot be checked against how conditions might have changed over time
The people checking the claim are the same people selling the product
The claim may not hold once conditions differ from the one tested
items.explain: Three separate weaknesses cost a reader three separate things. A missing date blocks comparison over time, an in-house test removes the outside check a reader would want, and a single named temperature limits how far the headline number can honestly be trusted.

items.stem: A buyer read only the desert-climate result from this article and concluded the tag was unreliable.  What did the buyer's conclusion get wrong?
choices: It treated one result as a verdict on the tag, when the article shows the climate, not the tag, is what changed.
It assumed heat could never affect a battery's performance at all.
It assumed the desert test used a different, weaker tag than the coastal and freezing mountain tests.
It assumed nineteen days in the desert was longer than the maker's own thirty-day claim.

distractorRationale.1: The buyer's mistake is not disbelieving that heat affects batteries; heat genuinely does affect this battery, exactly as the article explains.
distractorRationale.2: The article describes the same tag tested in three different climates, not three different tags.
distractorRationale.3: Nineteen days is shorter than the maker's thirty-day claim, not longer; that comparison is not where this buyer's error lies.

items.explain: A single result, read alone, looks like a verdict on the device itself.  The article's whole argument is that the tag stayed constant across all three tests and only the surrounding climate changed, which is exactly the context a one-test reading throws away.

items.stem: Which of these is the best summary of the article's advice to a buyer?
choices: Trust a maker's own test over an independent review board's test.
Buy the tag with the highest published runtime number, since a bigger number is always more reliable.
Avoid every tracking tag, since none of them can be trusted in any climate.
Ask what climate a runtime number was tested in before you trust it.

distractorRationale.0: The article gives no reason to prefer a maker's test over an independent one; if anything, its own review-board test is offered as the more trustworthy comparison.
distractorRationale.1: The article specifically warns that a maker's own test tends to produce the best possible number rather than a typical one, so treating the biggest number as automatically the most reliable is the mistake it argues against.
distractorRationale.2: The article never recommends avoiding tracking tags altogether; its advice is about how to read a number, not whether to use the product.

items.explain: The article does not tell a buyer which tag to choose or which number is biggest. It tells a buyer to ask a question first, what climate was this number measured in, before deciding whether that number applies to their own situation.

items.stem: In the tag report in this level, heat is the weather of the desert test, wearing a battery down.  Where does heat come into this tunnel article?
choices: The beacon's battery warms the granite around it, so the first tunnel held longest
The third tunnel ran warmest, which is why its signal faded after fifty-one minutes
The sharp bend in the second tunnel heats the signal until contact is lost
Water in the rock turns part of the signal into heat, which is how wet rock costs range

distractorRationale.0: The article never says the battery warms the rock.  The first tunnel held because it was dry and almost straight, not because of heat.
distractorRationale.1: No tunnel's temperature is given.  The article explains its results by water, the shape of the path, and depth, not by how warm a tunnel ran.
distractorRationale.2: The article says nothing about heat at the bend.  Heat comes in only in the paragraph on water, which says water is extremely good at turning a signal into heat.

items.explain: The same word does a different job in each report.  In the tag report heat is weather that wears a battery down;  in this article heat is where a signal's energy goes when water in the rock absorbs it, and that is how wet rock costs a beacon its range.

items.stem: Put the steps of this article's argument in the order it makes them.
tiles: Explain the three separate ways climate drains a battery
Report what the same tag did in three different climates
Tell a buyer to ask what temperature a number was measured at
Point out that read together, the results show the tag never changed
items.explain: The article does not open with its advice. distractorRationale.0: The gone silent column has three rows, not one.  Two tags stopped at about sixty hours and the other two ran on into day three, so the four did not stop together.
distractorRationale.1: Sixty-eight hours is under three days, and the claim written at the head of the log is thirty days.  You read the largest number in the column as though it had beaten that claim.
distractorRationale.4: The only thirty-day number on this page is the maker's claim at the head.  Everything the staff measured stopped inside three days, and the longest of it is just past sixty-eight hours.

items.explain: A log's columns are built to be read across, one line at a time, and each line here pairs an entry in the tags column with the point it fell silent.  Read that way the page gives three separate results rather than one, and the largest of the three is still counted in hours.  The thirty days at the head is the number under test, not a result the staff got.
items.whyTheFigureIsNeeded: The prose tells the cold-weather story in sentences, and only the drawing pairs each entry in the tags column with its own silence time on a line a reader can check straight across, with the brief's thirty days sitting at the head as the number under test.

items.stem: Two of the three tunnels on the memo are limestone.  Read what the memo gives under both of them.  What do those two tunnels show when they are set side by side?
choices: The same rock gave very different results: eight minutes in the wet tunnel and fifty-one in the dry.
Limestone is the worst rock a beacon can be tested in, whatever else is true of the tunnel.
The beacon carried into the limestone tunnels must have been a weaker beacon than the one used in granite.
The two limestone tunnels come out the same, which shows the rock is the only thing that counts.

distractorRationale.1: The article never says limestone is worse than granite.  It says wet rock absorbs radio energy far more effectively than dry rock does, and the memo's own dry limestone tunnel held for fifty-one minutes.
distractorRationale.2: The memo carries the line that rules this out: the beacon is not the thing that changed.  The same beacon test ran in all three tunnels, so a difference between tunnels cannot be a difference in the beacon.
distractorRationale.3: The memo gives "eight minutes" under one limestone tunnel and "fifty-one minutes" under the other, so the two do not come out the same.  The article also sets shape and depth beside water.

items.explain: Setting the two limestone tunnels side by side is what makes the point.  The rock is limestone in both, so limestone cannot be the thing that changed the answer.  What differs in the rock row is that one is wet and one is dry, and the shape row differs too, a sharp bend against a gentle curve.  The memo gives "eight minutes" under the wet, sharply bent one and "fifty-one minutes" under the dry one with a gentle curve.  Reading a single tunnel on its own is how a condition gets mistaken for a verdict on the rock.
items.whyTheFigureIsNeeded: The memo strips out every depth and every footage the article carries and leaves rock, shape and result aligned under each tunnel, so the two limestone tunnels can be compared property by property; the article scatters those same facts through one narrative paragraph and never sets the second tunnel against the third.

items.stem: The memo gives a temperature and a runtime under each of its three climates.  Choose the three statements the memo supports.
choices: The tag ran twenty-six days where the temperatures were in the fifties
The tag ran the same number of days in every climate
A different tag was used in each of the three climates
The tag ran nineteen days where the heat was above ninety degrees
The shortest runtime on the memo, just under three days, is the one in the freezing mountain column
The tag ran twenty-six days where the heat was above ninety degrees

distractorRationale.1: The memo gives "twenty-six days", "nineteen days", and just under three days.  Runtimes that far apart are not the same number of days, which is why all three results together say more than any one of them.
distractorRationale.2: The memo carries "the same tracking tag" at its head, and the article says outright that the tag did not change between tests.  The climate changed instead, which is the finding.
distractorRationale.5: The hottest air on the memo is above ninety degrees, and the runtime under it is nineteen days, which is shorter than the twenty-six days measured in the fifties.  The longest runtime on the memo belongs to the mild coastal column, not the hottest one.

items.explain: The memo has two things to say under each climate, a temperature and a runtime, and every statement worth choosing pairs one with the other.  Twenty-six days belongs with the fifties, nineteen days with the heat above ninety degrees, and the shortest runtime of all with the freezing mountain.  The wrong choices each deny something the memo gives: that the runtimes differ, that one tag ran in all three tests, and that heat cost the tag time rather than winning it time.
items.whyTheFigureIsNeeded: Each correct statement is a pairing of a temperature with the runtime measured at it, and the memo is the only place those two sit in the same column; the article puts each temperature and its runtime in separate sentences and then spends its remaining paragraphs on how to read the three together, so the pairings have to be reassembled from prose rather than read off.

items.stem: The memo's result row gives "fifty-one minutes" under one of the tunnels.  Read that row across.  Then read what the article says about the first tunnel.  Put the three tunnels in order, from the longest hold down to the shortest.
tiles: the first tunnel
the second tunnel
the third tunnel
items.explain: The memo names the tunnels first, second, and third, and that is not the order of the results.  The first tunnel is the one where the beacon ran the full life of the battery, and the article says it beat the second by more than an hour, so its hold is the longest.  The third tunnel's fifty-one minutes comes next, and the second tunnel's eight minutes is last.  Taking the printed order for the ranking is the mistake this item is built on.
items.whyTheFigureIsNeeded: The article ranks only the first hold against the second and never puts all three in one order; it reports each one inside its own tunnel's sentences, separated by depths, a bend measurement and a reference to the Halloway log.  The memo is the only place the three results stand in one line under headings that can be ordered, so the table fixes the bottom two and the article settles the first.

items.stem: Finish the reading of the memo.  Its temperatures row runs in the fifties, then above ninety degrees, then freezing, and in the same order its runtime row runs {{0}}.  Read both rows together and the memo shows that {{1}}.

choices: just under three days, then nineteen days, then twenty-six days
the same twenty-six days in every climate, whether mild, hot or freezing
twenty-six days, then nineteen days, then just under three days
the hottest test is not the shortest one, because the freezing test is shorter still
the tag ran longest in the hottest air of the three, above ninety degrees
a broken tag must have been used for the desert test and not the others

items.explain: Both rows read together say more than either says alone.  The temperatures climb from the fifties to above ninety degrees and then fall to freezing, while the runtime shortens at every step, from twenty-six days to nineteen days to just under three.  Heat costs the tag time and freezing costs it far more, which is why the memo's own line says "a number describes one climate, not every climate".
items.whyTheFigureIsNeeded: The answer is a comparison of one whole row against another, in the memo's own left-to-right order, and only the memo puts the three temperatures in one line above the three runtimes.  A reader working from the article alone has to hold six separate values from one long paragraph, split across six sentences, before the pattern appears.
